title: Compliance automation software: which kind fixes which problem?
description: What compliance automation software does for a SOC 2, ISO 27001 or HIPAA audit, what it costs small firms, and what your team still owns.
job: choose compliance automation software for a first or second SOC 2, ISO 27001 or HIPAA audit at a 40-500 person firm
verdict: Buy an audit-readiness platform for SOC 2 evidence, but an independent CPA firm still performs the audit.[^8][^1]
Treat list prices as floors: no AWS Marketplace listing we read prices a firm above 100 employees, by our count.[^10][^12]
By our count, 13 of SOC 2's 33 common criteria need a named person's judgment.[^2][^1]
Platforms collect evidence but don't run your controls:[^1] access control drew exceptions in 51% of 75 examinations.[^7]
Hire the auditor yourself: AICPA says business ties between auditors and tool vendors can threaten independence.[^3][^5]

summary: Audit-readiness platforms gather security evidence, while regulatory-change and anti-money laundering (AML) tools serve banks and insurers.[^8][^23] Vendors say their platforms test your systems against System and Organization Controls (SOC) 2 or another framework and flag gaps.[^9] An independent certified public accountant (CPA) firm still issues the report.[^1]

recipes.name: 1. Under 100 staff, first SOC 2 for one big customer
recipes.when: Pick one audit-readiness platform and one framework, and choose the CPA firm yourself.[^10][^4] Secureframe and Sprinto both list bands up to 100 employees.[^10][^11]
flow: Head of IT: list the systems that hold customer data, as the audit scope
Head of IT: connect cloud, identity, HR and code systems to the platform
COO: give every control the platform lists a named owner
Security lead: adapt the template policies, and leadership approves them
Head of IT: fix flagged gaps before the observation window starts
COO: engage an independent CPA firm after checking its peer review
Control owners: answer the auditor's extra evidence requests
recipes.cost: Secureframe lists $15,000 a year with one framework and Sprinto $9,500, by our math.[^10][^11] Drata puts a small or midsize firm's Type 2 audit fee at $12,000 to $20,000 on top (vendor figure).[^13]

recipes.name: 2. 100 to 500 staff, several frameworks
recipes.when: Price per framework and per employee band, because every published band stops at 100 staff.[^9][^10] GRC staff at firms of 250 to 1,500 people manage 8 frameworks on average, per a Drata vendor survey of 300 IT and security professionals.[^21]
flow: COO: list every framework customers ask for, with the deal that asked
Head of IT: map shared controls once, so one piece of evidence serves several frameworks
Head of compliance: get a written quote at your real headcount and framework count
Control owners: clear the exceptions the platform flags each week
Head of IT: give the platform read-only, least-privilege access
recipes.cost: Drata lists $25,000 for a 100-person platform plus $7,500 per framework.[^9] Drata's example: about $75,000 for a 100-employee firm's first SOC 2 Type 2 alone, with audit, platform, pen test and outside help (vendor figure).[^13]

recipes.name: 3. Bank, credit union or insurer
recipes.when: Start with regulatory change and anti-money laundering work, which our page for bank and insurer compliance teams covers.[^23] Add a SOC 2 platform when customers start asking for the report.[^22]
flow: Chief compliance officer: rank the obligations that cost the most hours
Chief compliance officer: pick regulatory-change and AML tools for those first
Head of IT: add an audit-readiness platform when customers ask for SOC 2
Vendor manager: review the platform like any critical vendor
recipes.cost: The same listings apply if customers also want SOC 2: Sprinto's comes to $9,500 with one framework, by our math.[^11] Regulatory-change and AML tool costs sit on our compliance-teams page.[^23]

humanRole: The head of IT or security owns the risk assessment and control design. AICPA warns that a tool's template control list can miss risks unique to your firm.[^1][^2]

We'd have a named control owner approve every questionnaire answer; even Drata says owners must check low-confidence matches and sensitive evidence.[^15] Generative AI can state false content confidently.[^24]

Under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), you must name a security official and run a risk analysis.[^18] After a ransomware breach, one health plan paid $245,000 in April 2026, and HHS found it had no accurate risk analysis.[^19]
An independent CPA firm you choose tests the evidence and issues the SOC 2 opinion. It may not merely sign a report a tool generated.[^1][^3]

ownData.title: How much of SOC 2 can a platform actually do?
ownData.intro: By our count, a platform can pull system evidence for 10 of SOC 2's 33 common criteria, while 13 need a named person's judgment.[^2][^1] The other 10 need a document a person writes or approves, which the platform stores and tracks.[^2] On 28 Nov 2026 we sorted each criterion in AICPA's 2017 Trust Services Criteria (TSC) by its main burden; 2027 drafts are open for comment.[^2][^6]
headers: Documents a person writes or approves
rows: CC1.1 ethics, CC1.3 structure, CC1.4 competence, CC1.5 accountability
CC2.1 quality information, CC2.2 internal, CC2.3 external
CC3.1 objectives, CC3.2 risks, CC3.3 fraud, CC3.4 changes
CC6.1, CC6.2, CC6.3 access; CC6.6 boundary; CC6.7 transmission; CC6.8 malware
CC7.3 event triage, CC7.4 response, CC7.5 recovery
CC9.1 disruption risk, CC9.2 vendor risk
ownData.note: Limits: this is our sort, not AICPA's; each criterion sits under its main burden, and your auditor decides what evidence is enough.[^2][^1] In one CPA firm's 75 examinations, access control (51%), change management (41%) and logging (37%) drew the most exceptions, all system-evidence areas by our mapping.[^7] Yet the misses it lists include skipped access reviews and unreviewed alerts, which our sort keeps as human sign-offs.[^7]

example.input: Illustrative: a 120-person software firm stalls on a deal because the buyer's security team wants a SOC 2 Type 2 report. The head of IT keeps evidence as screenshots in folders, and nobody owns the quarterly access reviews.
example.output: After: a platform pulls access, device and change-ticket evidence and flags missed reviews, while named owners approve the policies and the risk assessment.[^9][^1] Drata's listing covers 100 full-time staff, so its $32,500 for SOC 2 is a floor at 120, by our math.[^9] An independent CPA firm tests it after a 3 to 12 month observation window, which can push a first Type 2 past 9 months.[^7]

watchOuts: Buying the tool as if it were the audit: some vendors promise compliance in weeks or hours, a term SOC 2 never uses.[^4] Fix: plan for 3 to 9 months end to end, and longer for a first Type 2 with its observation window.[^7]
Template controls nobody owns: AICPA says relying only on a tool's predefined controls can miss your risks and lead to a modified opinion.[^1] Fix: give each control a named owner who adapts it.[^2]
An auditor tied to the tool vendor: AICPA ethics staff say such arrangements can raise significant threats to independence.[^3] Fix: choose the CPA firm yourself, and check its peer review.[^4][^5]

Trusting AI-drafted answers unchecked: Vanta claims a 95% acceptance rate (vendor claim),[^14] but NIST says generative AI can confidently state false content.[^24] Fix: have an owner approve every answer, not only the low-confidence matches Drata routes to people.[^15]

Broad platform access without a vendor review: a May 2025 Vanta bug exposed integration metadata from under 20% of its integrations to other customers.[^16] Fix: give it least-privilege access and the due diligence the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) expects for mission-critical vendors.[^17]

faq.q: How much does compliance automation software cost?
faq.a: Published AWS list prices run from $9,500 to $32,500 a year with one framework, by our math, for firms of 100 staff or fewer.[^11][^9] The audit is extra: Drata puts a small or midsize firm's Type 2 audit fee at $12,000 to $20,000 (vendor figure).[^13]

faq.q: Does the software do the SOC 2 audit for us?
faq.a: No, because only an independent CPA firm can examine your controls and issue a SOC 2 report.[^1][^4] AICPA says using a tool doesn't change the auditor's responsibilities.[^1]

faq.q: Will our auditor accept evidence the platform collects?
faq.a: Yes, once the auditor has tested that the tool's output is reliable, since AICPA treats it as information management must stand behind.[^1] Expect follow-ups: 88% of one CPA firm's 75 examinations needed extra evidence.[^7]

faq.q: Can AI fill in security questionnaires for us?
faq.a: Yes, as a first draft, though Drata says control owners must still check low-confidence matches and sensitive evidence.[^15] We'd have them check every answer, since Vanta's 95% acceptance rate is a vendor claim.[^14]

faq.q: Is it safe to connect a compliance platform to our systems?
faq.a: Yes, with least-privilege access and the due diligence FINRA expects for any mission-critical vendor.[^17] Vanta's own report describes a May 2025 bug that showed some integration metadata to other customers.[^16]

faq.q: Can we use the auditor the platform recommends?
faq.a: Yes, if you confirm the firm is independent of the platform and check its peer review results.[^4][^3] AICPA told peer reviewers in 2026 to flag identical reports and risk assessments across clients.[^5]

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy for SOC 2, ISO 27001 and HIPAA readiness, because every AWS Marketplace listing we read sells evidence connectors and framework mappings ready-made.[^9][^8] In MIT NANDA's interviews with 52 organizations about generative AI tools, external partnerships reached deployment about 67% of the time, internal builds about 33%.[^20]
buyVsBuild.build: Build only the glue: an export from a system the platform can't reach, or a spreadsheet if you hold one framework and few systems. AICPA expects management to check the accuracy and completeness of whatever the tool produces.[^1]

pickElse: Only one customer asked, and a short questionnaire will do: answer it from a reviewed answer library.[^15] Nearly 70% of 255 security, compliance and IT professionals in a Secureframe vendor survey say their firms prove security through questionnaires and requests for proposal.[^22]
You're a bank, credit union or insurer buried in new rules and alerts: start with the regulatory-change and AML tools on our compliance-teams page.[^23]
You handle health data but no customer has asked for SOC 2: start with the HIPAA risk analysis the rule requires.[^18] Regulators enforce it, as April 2026's settlements show.[^19]

sources.name: AICPA staff, FAQs: Effect of the use of software tools on SOC 2 examinations (nonauthoritative, as of 30 Jun 2021), PDF via AICPA's asset host
sources.what: A service organization's use of a SOC 2 tool "does not change the responsibilities of the service auditor". Information a tool generates is information provided by the entity (IPE): management evaluates its accuracy and completeness, and the auditor evaluates its reliability (AT-C 205.35). Management is responsible for identifying and assessing risks and for designing, implementing, operating and monitoring controls; it "may not be able to rely solely on predefined or standardized control listings embedded in a SOC 2 tool", and overreliance could lead to a modified opinion. A tool's risk-assessment function alone can miss unique technologies. The auditor should be independent of a tool provider that is a responsible party, and it would not be appropriate for an auditor to merely sign a report a tool generated. AICPA republished these FAQs on 31 Mar 2026 behind a free account; we read the AICPA-hosted 2021 PDF. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: AICPA, 2017 Trust Services Criteria (With Revised Points of Focus, 2022), PDF via AICPA's asset host
sources.what: AICPA's own public copy; its landing page needs a free account. The criteria a SOC 2 examination reports against, set by AICPA's Assurance Services Executive Committee. The common criteria for Security run CC1.1 to CC9.2: control environment (CC1), information and communication (CC2), risk assessment (CC3, including CC3.2 risk identification and CC3.3 fraud), monitoring (CC4), control activities (CC5), logical and physical access (CC6), system operations (CC7), change management (CC8) and risk mitigation (CC9, including CC9.2 vendor and business partner risk). Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: AICPA Professional Ethics Division, Ethics Staff Insights: Business arrangements with SOC tool providers (Apr 2026)
sources.what: AICPA members increasingly enter business arrangements with SOC 2 tool providers, and "these relationships can raise significant threats to compliance with the Code of Professional Conduct", including independence and objectivity. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: Journal of Accountancy, Promises of 'fast and easy' threaten SOC credibility (1 Feb 2026)
sources.what: SOC tool vendors, "now numbering in the dozens", may promise compliance ("a term never used in SOC 2 examinations") "in mere weeks — or even just hours". Most tool providers are not CPA firms and cannot attest that controls are effective. Advice to clients: vet the CPA firm, including its peer review results; ask about scope, sampling and how the firm maintains its independence; and ask whether the offer is unrealistically fast, easy or cheap. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: Journal of Accountancy, AICPA guides peer reviewers to address SOC 2 risks (14 May 2026)
sources.what: AICPA's vice president for ethics and firm quality: "Some firms are leaning too heavily on third-party SOC platforms without applying the professional judgment required by our standards." Engagements with identical reports, risk assessments, sample sizes and testing procedures are not performed under the standards and are "nonconforming" in peer review. Reviewers look at a firm's use of external SOC platforms, the reasonableness of timelines and whether work is tailored to each client. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: Journal of Accountancy, AICPA publishes proposed updates to SOC 2 description criteria (17 Nov 2026)
sources.what: AICPA published exposure drafts of the 2027 SOC 2 description criteria and SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria; comments on both are accepted through 15 Jan 2027. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: Lazarus Alliance, 2026 SOC 2 Audit Benchmark Report (Aug 2026)
sources.what: A CPA firm's own data on N = 75 completed SOC 2 examinations, Jan 2025 to Jun 2026: 55 Type 2 and 20 Type 1; 32 first-time and 43 renewals. Formal fieldwork typically 6-10 weeks; end to end 3 to 9 months; a Type 2 observation period of 3-12 months comes on top. 71% (53 of 75) had at least one exception: 84% of first-time examinations vs 60% of renewals. 88% (66 of 75) needed at least one round of additional evidence (93% of Type 2). Average about 1,450 evidence artifacts (Type 2 about 1,650). Exception areas: access control and user provisioning 51%, change management 41%, logging, monitoring and alerting 37%, risk assessment and vendor management 32%, system description accuracy 28%, security configuration and vulnerability management 24%, incident response and continuity testing 19%. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: Drata, How Much Does a SOC 2 Audit Cost? (25 Mar 2026)
sources.what: Vendor figures. Audit fee alone: Type 1 $7,500 to $15,000 for small to midsize companies; Type 2 $12,000 to $20,000 for small to midsize companies and $30,000 to $100,000+ for large organizations. Total first year $25,000 for a small startup to over $200,000; a 100-employee mid-size company's first-year SOC 2 Type 2 scenario comes to about $75,000, including a mid-tier audit, a platform, pen testing and some consultant support. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: Vanta, Vanta AI product page
sources.what: Vendor claim: Vanta suggests security questionnaire answers from your knowledge base and previous responses "with a 95% acceptance rate. Just review and submit!" Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: Drata, Security Questionnaire Automation (13 Feb 2026)
sources.what: Human reviewers are prompted to confirm or adjust matches below a set confidence threshold. "Control owners should still validate low-confidence matches, clarify ambiguous questions, and approve sensitive evidence before sharing." Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: Vanta, Root Cause Analysis of Product Bug (Inc-868) (13 Jun 2025)
sources.what: Vanta's own disclosure: a code change deployed on 22 May 2025 caused a subset of data from less than 20% of its third-party integrations to be written into other customers' tenants. Fewer than 4% of Vanta customers were affected. The data could include metadata about employee security training, tool access, devices and vulnerabilities; no passwords, MFA credentials or API keys. Full remediation was completed on 3 Jun 2025. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: FINRA, 2026 Annual Regulatory Oversight Report: Third-Party Risk Landscape
sources.what: Effective practices for member firms: assess a vendor's use of GenAI; add contract language that keeps firm or customer sensitive information out of a vendor's open-source GenAI tool; keep an inventory of firm data types vendors access; enforce least-privilege identity access controls; revoke vendor access when the relationship ends. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: eCFR, 45 CFR 164.308, HIPAA Security Rule administrative safeguards
sources.what: Risk analysis (Required): "Conduct an accurate and thorough assessment of the potential risks and vulnerabilities" to electronic protected health information. Assigned security responsibility: "Identify the security official who is responsible for the development and implementation of the policies and procedures." Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: HHS, Office for Civil Rights settles four HIPAA Security Rule ransomware investigations (23 Apr 2026)
sources.what: Four settlements paid a total of $1,165,000; 13 completed investigations in OCR's Risk Analysis Initiative. SG Health Plan failed to conduct an accurate and thorough risk analysis and paid $245,000; RWHG paid $320,000. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: MIT NANDA, The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 (Jul 2025)
sources.what: MIT no longer hosts the report (its link now opens the NANDA project page, checked 26 Nov 2026); copy hosted by MLQ.ai. Sample: 52 organizations interviewed, survey of 153 leaders, and 300+ public AI initiatives reviewed. $30-40 billion of enterprise GenAI investment; 95% of organizations are getting zero return; just 5% of integrated AI pilots extract millions in value. Task-specific tools: 60% of organizations evaluated them, 20% piloted, 5% reached production. Over 80% of organizations explored or piloted ChatGPT or Copilot, and nearly 40% report deployment. External partnerships with customized tools reached deployment about 67% of the time vs about 33% for internal builds: 2x as likely, twice the success rate. Only 40% of companies purchased an official LLM subscription; workers at over 90% of companies surveyed use personal AI tools for work. For mission-critical work, 90% of users prefer humans. Enterprises, defined as firms with over $100 million in annual revenue, lead in pilot count but report the lowest pilot-to-scale conversion. Read 26 Nov 2026.

sources.name: Drata, The State of GRC 2025 (Wakefield Research survey)
sources.what: Survey of 300 US IT and security professionals at companies with 250 to 1,500 employees, conducted by Wakefield Research for Drata, Nov-Dec 2024. GRC staff manage an average of 8 compliance frameworks, and 60% manage at least five. Manual work takes 14 hours a week on average. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: Secureframe, 2026 Cybersecurity & Compliance Benchmark report release
sources.what: Survey of 255 security, compliance and IT professionals, Oct 2025 (vendor survey). Teams spend 8 hours a week on compliance tasks; 68% of organizations have one or fewer full-time cybersecurity staff; 61% say compliance was required to win or renew contracts; 47% say lacking certification delayed sales. Nearly 70% rely on security questionnaires and requests for proposal to prove security posture. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: Zavient, Where should a bank or insurer compliance team start with AI?
sources.what: Our page for bank and insurer compliance teams: regulatory change management, complaints, Bank Secrecy Act and anti-money laundering (BSA/AML) work, model risk and what examiners accept, with the compliance officer and BSA officer as the decision owners. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: NIST AI 600-1, Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (Jul 2024)
sources.what: Confabulation: "The production of confidently stated but erroneous or false content", by which users may be misled. Automation bias, excessive deference to automated systems, can make it worse. Read 28 Nov 2026.

answers.recipes: Firms under 100 staff fit one platform and one framework, while larger firms should price per framework and banks should start with regulatory change.[^10][^9][^23]
answers.human-role: Management owns the risk assessment, control design, policy approval and deficiency calls, and an independent CPA firm issues the opinion.[^1][^4]
answers.example: SOC 2 examinations ran 3 to 9 months end to end across one CPA firm's 75, with first-time and Type 2 examinations taking longer.[^7]
answers.what-goes-wrong: Teams go wrong by treating the tool as the audit, keeping template controls nobody owns, and letting the vendor steer the choice of auditor.[^1][^5]
answers.something-else: Pick neither when one customer wants a short questionnaire, or when your real burden is bank or insurer regulation rather than a security audit.[^22][^23]

offer.heading: Not sure which kind of tool your audit needs?
offer.body: Often one platform plus named control owners is enough, and sometimes a reviewed questionnaire library is. Bring the customer's security request, and in a free 30-minute diagnostic we sort what a platform can pull from what your team owns. You leave with a pick and a first step.

reviews.notes: Read as the COO of a 150-person software firm whose biggest prospect wants a SOC 2 Type 2. The bottom line answers in order: buy a platform, treat prices as floors, people keep the judgment, automation is not the audit, pick the auditor yourself. Recipe 2 names my size band and says to get a written quote, since no listing prices it. FAQ questions come from the People Also Ask box and vendor FAQs (cost, does it do the audit, will the auditor accept it, AI questionnaires, safety, platform-recommended auditor); no forums cited. Demand: 'compliance automation software' 320 a month at $113.49, KD 17; 'compliance automation' 320; 'compliance automation tools' 140. Reframe pass: the problem-to-tool table answers what I would ask first.

Reads on a phone. SOC, CPA, AICPA, TSC, GRC, AWS, AML, KYC, BSA, HIPAA, FINRA and NIST checked: each is spelled out or a named body. ISO 27001 is named as a standard, not spelled out; PCI DSS is not used in body text. Recipe flows name the role on every step. Cut the regulatory-change and AML rows to a pointer at the sibling page so the two pages don't compete. Reframe pass: every row says who signs off.

Wants the year-one bill. Table 2 gives five dated AWS list prices with their employee bands, and recipe costs add Drata's vendor audit-fee range and its 100-employee first-year example, both labelled vendor figures. No Zavient price. Reframe pass: the 'floors' line keeps me from budgeting off a 1-20 employee price.

Read as the head of IT and security who will run the platform. Own-data table matches how the work splits in practice: access, change and monitoring evidence pulls; risk, deficiency, incident and vendor calls don't. Moved CC7.5 (recovery) from documents to judgments after rereading the criterion: root cause and restore decisions are the burden, not the test record. Added read-only, least-privilege access as a recipe step, with Vanta's own incident report and FINRA's practice as the reason. Reframe pass: the cross-check (51% access-control exceptions) is the line I'd forward.

Steve decides from the title and bottom line. Five bullets of 20 words or fewer, two sources each. He'd distrust a vendor ranking; the page ranks no vendor and labels every claim. No audit or consulting firm is listed as a provider; Lazarus Alliance appears only as a data source. The vendor-misconduct allegation story was cut (see sourceCheck). The offer says what he leaves with: a pick and a first step. Reframe pass: no price added.
